---
title: "Case study: the shape of rock crabs"
---

# Introduction

In this case study, we put Chapters 2 to 4 to work on a single data set, from the research
question to the comparison of models. In the chapters, the order was always the same: a
concept first, then an example chosen to illustrate it. Here we turn that around. We start
with an ecological question and a data set, and we pick from the course whatever tools help
us answer it. There is no new theory on this page. You will see the many small decisions
that one has to make to analyse data: which variable to analyse, which distributions are
worth trying, which models to compare and how to read the results. It is important to
remember that there is no single way of analysing a data set, even when you are asking the
same question. But there are some general principles that will help you build a
well-founded and robust analysis of complex data, and I hope to illustrate them with this
case study.

We start with a research question that these data could answer, and follow with an
exploratory data analysis that helps us decide which variables to analyse and which models
to use. From that point onwards we will follow the recipe for a fit at the end of
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-aic)
(write the model, write the NLL, fit it, check it, quantify the uncertainty, compare the
models).

# The data

The data come from a study of two species of rock crab of the genus *Leptograpsus* on the
coast of Western Australia, by Campbell and Mahon.^[Campbell, N. A. and Mahon, R. J. (1974).
A multivariate study of variation in two species of rock crab of the genus *Leptograpsus*.
*Australian Journal of Zoology* 22: 417–425. The data set is distributed with the package
`MASS` of Venables, W. N. and Ripley, B. D. (2002), *Modern Applied Statistics with S*,
fourth edition, Springer.] The two species look very much alike except for their colour,
and they are known as the **blue form** and the **orange form**. For a long time they were
regarded as colour variants of a single species, *Leptograpsus variegatus*. Shortly before
this study, ecological and genetic work by the second author showed that they are two
distinct species, which live side by side on the same shores but differ in their ecology
and behaviour. To add to that evidence and to help with the identification of the two
species, they set up a study to quantify the morphology of the crabs.

The study measured 50 males and 50 females of each species, 200 crabs in total, collected
at Fremantle, Western Australia. The crabs were collected at night and captured on sight as
the collector moved along the sampling area, and the same person (Mahon) collected and
measured all of them with vernier callipers, to the nearest 0.1 mm. The data are available
as the data set `crabs` of the package `MASS`, which is installed with every copy of R, so
you do not need to install anything. We load the data as usual and look at the first rows:

```{r}
# Measurements of 200 rock crabs (see ?MASS::crabs).
data(crabs, package = "MASS")
head(crabs)
```

The columns are:

- `sp`: the species, `B` for the blue form and `O` for the orange form;
- `sex`: `F` for female and `M` for male;
- `index`: the number of the crab within its group, from 1 to 50 (an identifier, not a
  measurement);
- `FL`: the width of the frontal region of the carapace, which the authors call the front
  lip (mm);
- `RW`: the width of the rear of the carapace (mm);
- `CL`: the length of the carapace along its midline (mm);
- `CW`: the maximum width of the carapace (mm);
- `BD`: the depth of the body (mm). In females, the abdomen was moved aside to measure it.

The carapace is the shell that covers the back of a crab, so four of the five measurements
describe its outline as seen from above. @fig-crabs-carapace, from the original article,
shows where each of them was taken.

![Dorsal view of the carapace of *Leptograpsus*, showing the four carapace measurements: the width of the frontal region just in front of the frontal tubercles (FL), the width of the rear of the carapace (RW), the length along the midline (CL) and the maximum width (CW). Reproduced from Figure 1 of Campbell and Mahon (1974), *Australian Journal of Zoology* 22: 417–425.](images/carapace-measurements.png){#fig-crabs-carapace width="45%" fig-alt="Line drawing of a crab carapace seen from above, with arrows marking the maximum width (CW) across the widest part, the width of the front (FL) across the front lip, the length (CL) along the midline from front to back, and the rear width (RW) across the back edge."}

Because the measurements were recorded to the nearest 0.1 mm, strictly speaking
they can only take values on a grid with steps of 0.1 mm. These steps are tiny compared with
the differences between crabs, so we treat the measurements as continuous, as we did in
[Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-continuous_measurements) with the flipper lengths of
the penguins.

# The research question

Every analysis starts with a question, and it is worth being honest about this: the same
data set can answer many different questions, and each of them leads to a different
analysis. The data that we use here are five measurements of the body of 200 rock crabs of
two species and both sexes. With these data we could ask, for example:

- How do the different parts of the body grow relative to each other as a crab gets
  bigger? This is the question of **allometry**, and it is about the relationships between
  the measurements.
- How large is the **sexual dimorphism** (i.e., how much do the bodies of males and females
  differ), and does it depend on the species and on the measurement that we use?
- How do the two species differ in the shape of their body? This was the original question
  of the paper.

Each of these three questions leads to different response variables, a different model and a
different model comparison, so you cannot do "the analysis" of a data set without first
deciding which question you are asking. It also means that you cannot simply ask an AI
assistant to "analyse my data": that would let the AI decide for you what you want to learn
from the data.

Ideally you decide on the question before you collect the data, because the question also
determines the data collection: what to measure, on how many individuals and in which
groups. Choosing the question after looking at the data has a less obvious problem. Any
sample has accidental features (Chapter 4 made this point about models with many
parameters), and if you go looking for the most interesting pattern in a data set, you will
probably find some of them and mistake them for a general ecological pattern. Looking at the
data to decide how to answer a question is fine and we will do a lot of it below; changing
the question to fit what the data show is where the trouble starts.

In this case study we ask: **to what extent can we tell apart the two species and the two
sexes of these crabs from a few measurements taken with callipers?** That is, how large are
the differences in body shape between the species and between the sexes, compared with the
variation among the crabs of each group?

Why would anyone care? For the two species, the question has a real history. Once the blue
and the orange forms were recognised as separate species, the old museum specimens to which
the existing names of these crabs are attached had to be examined, to decide which name
belongs to which species. However, crabs that have been preserved in chemicals lose their
colour, so these specimens could not be identified by the one feature that everyone used to
tell the species apart. Campbell and Mahon collected these data precisely to find a way of
identifying the species independently of colour, and a clear difference in body shape would
also add to the evidence that the two forms are separate species. The same need exists in
the field: colour is a judgement made by eye, on which different observers (or the same
observer in different light) may not agree, whereas a measurement with callipers is quick,
cheap and repeatable.

Sex enters the question for two reasons. The first is practical: to sex a crab you have to
catch it and turn it over to look at its underside, so measurements that identify the sex
would be useful as well. The second is that sexual dimorphism gets in the way of comparing
the species. If males and females differ in shape, a description of a species that mixes
the two sexes describes neither of them well, so we have to take sex into account to see the
differences between the species clearly (this is also where the design of the study helps,
as we will see in the next section).

Note how the question is phrased. We do not ask "is there a significant difference between
the species?", because with enough crabs almost any difference will be detected and the
answer tells us nothing about whether the measurements are useful. We ask how large the
differences are compared with the variation within each group, because that is what
determines how well the measurements can tell the groups apart. This is a question about
whole distributions, and distributions are exactly what Chapters 2 to 4 taught us to
describe, fit and compare. Campbell and Mahon answered their version of the question with
multivariate methods that combine all five measurements at once, which are beyond this
course. We will use the tools of Chapters 2 to 4 instead, and at the end we will compare our
answer with theirs.

# Exploratory data analysis

To see how the crabs are distributed over the groups, we count them for every combination
of species and sex with `table()`, which you used in Chapter 3 to count seedlings in
quadrats. With two variables, `table()` counts the combinations and arranges them in rows
and columns:

```{r}
# Number of crabs for each combination of species (rows) and sex (columns).
table(crabs$sp, crabs$sex)
```

There are exactly 50 crabs of each sex in each species. This is a **balanced design**
with two factors (species and sex), and every combination of the two factors is
present. A design like this is what you would plan for our question: every group has the
same number of crabs, so every group is described with similar precision, and having all
four combinations allows us to look at the differences between the sexes within each
species (and the other way around). It also means that the numbers in the table were
fixed by the study, so they tell us nothing about how common each group is on the shore.

## A first look at the measurements

The natural first plot for comparing a measurement across groups is a boxplot, which you
met in the Chapter 1 practical. The formula `CW ~ sex + sp` asks for one box for every
combination of sex and species. We draw one panel per measurement, filling the boxes
with blue and orange for the two species. Before plotting, we store the colours (in the order
of the levels of `sp`, blue first) and, for later, the symbols that we will use for females
(open circles) and males (filled circles):

```{r}
# Colours for the blue and orange species, and symbols for females (open) and males
# (filled), in the order of the levels of sp and sex.
form_colours = c("#0072B2", "#E69F00")
sex_symbols = c(1, 19)
```

The plot itself loops over the five measurements. Inside the loop, `crabs[, measurements[i]]`
selects one column of the data frame by its name:

```{r}
#| label: fig-crabs-boxplots
#| fig-cap: "The five measurements of the crabs for each combination of sex (F, M) and species (B, O). Blue and orange boxes are the blue and the orange species."
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 9
# Names of the measurement columns and titles for the panels.
measurements = c("FL", "RW", "CL", "CW", "BD")
measurement_titles = c("Front lip width", "Rear width", "Carapace length",
                       "Carapace width", "Body depth")

# One panel per measurement; restore the graphics settings afterwards.
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (i in 1:5) {
  boxplot(crabs[, measurements[i]] ~ sex + sp, data = crabs,
          col = rep(form_colours, each = 2),
          main = measurement_titles[i],
          xlab = "Sex and species", ylab = "Length (mm)")
}
par(old_par)
```

The first thing to notice is how much the boxes overlap (this is why we need statistics).
In every group the crabs span a wide range of sizes, from about 15 mm to almost 50 mm of
carapace length, so the crabs in the data are of many different ages. There are some differences between the groups (the
blue females tend to be the smallest crabs and the orange females have a wider rear), but
they are small compared with the variation within each group. If we had to guess the group
of a crab from one of these measurements alone, we would be wrong very often.

We should also be careful with what these differences mean. A group of crabs with a larger
median carapace may contain larger animals because of its biology, or simply because more
large crabs of that group happened to be caught. The crabs were captured on sight, and we
do not know how the size of a crab affected its chance of being seen and caught, so
differences in overall size are a weak basis for an answer to our question.

## Relationships between the measurements

Because all five measurements were taken on the same crab, we can also look at how they
vary together. The function `pairs()`, which you used in the Chapter 1 practical on the
`iris` flowers, draws a scatter plot for every pair of measurements. We colour the points
by species and use the symbols for the sexes:

```{r}
#| label: fig-crabs-pairs
#| fig-cap: "Pairs of measurements of the 200 crabs (mm). Blue and orange points are the two species; open circles are females and filled circles are males."
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 8
# One scatter plot for every pair of measurements, coloured by species, with symbols by sex.
pairs(crabs[, measurements],
      labels = c("FL (mm)", "RW (mm)", "CL (mm)", "CW (mm)", "BD (mm)"),
      col = form_colours[as.numeric(crabs$sp)],
      pch = sex_symbols[as.numeric(crabs$sex)])
```

The points of every panel lie close to a line: a crab with a long carapace also has a wide
carapace, a deep body and a wide front lip. In the language of
[Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-two_continuous_variables), the measurements are
strongly **correlated**, and the reason is simple: they all grow as the crab grows. If our
question were about allometry, this is the figure we would study in detail. For our question
the strong correlation tells us something different, namely that the five measurements
mostly repeat the same information, the size of the crab.

Look more closely, though, and the groups separate within the panels. In the panel of the
front lip against the carapace width (first row, fourth column), the orange crabs lie
above the blue ones: at the same width of the carapace, an orange crab has a wider front
lip. In the panel of the rear width against the carapace length (second row, third column),
the open circles lie above the filled ones: at the same length, a female has a wider rear
than a male. In other words, the groups differ in the proportions of their bodies, their
shape, more clearly than in any single measurement. Their size mixes the shape with the age
of the crab, and the scatter plots take the age out by comparing crabs of the same size.

## From size to shape

A simple way to describe the shape of a crab with one number is the ratio of two
measurements. If two measurements grow in proportion, their ratio is the same for a small
and a large crab, so it removes the size and keeps the shape. Based on the scatter plots, we
calculate two ratios: the width of the front lip divided by the carapace width, which seemed
to separate the species, and the rear width divided by the carapace length, which seemed
to separate the sexes. A ratio of two lengths has no units.

We add the two ratios as new columns with `mutate()` from the package `dplyr`, as in the
Chapter 1 practical:

```{r}
#| message: false
library(dplyr)

# Front lip width relative to carapace width, and rear width relative to carapace length.
crabs = mutate(crabs,
               fl_cw_ratio = FL / CW,
               rw_cl_ratio = RW / CL)
```

We draw the two ratios with the same boxplots as before:

```{r}
#| label: fig-crabs-ratios
#| fig-cap: "Two ratios of measurements for each combination of sex (F, M) and species (B, O): the width of the front lip relative to the carapace width (left) and the rear width relative to the carapace length (right)."
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 9
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
boxplot(fl_cw_ratio ~ sex + sp, data = crabs, col = rep(form_colours, each = 2),
        xlab = "Sex and species", ylab = "Front lip / carapace width")
boxplot(rw_cl_ratio ~ sex + sp, data = crabs, col = rep(form_colours, each = 2),
        xlab = "Sex and species", ylab = "Rear width / carapace length")
par(old_par)
```

This looks very different from @fig-crabs-boxplots. The ratio of the front lip to the
carapace width separates the two species with hardly any overlap, while the two sexes
within each species are very similar. The ratio of the rear width to the carapace length does
the opposite: it separates the sexes and hardly differs between the species. To put
numbers on the difference between the groups and the variation within them, we calculate
the mean and the standard deviation of both ratios in each group with `group_by()` and
`summarise()`, again from the Chapter 1 practical:

```{r}
# Mean and standard deviation of the two ratios in each combination of species and sex.
crab_groups = group_by(crabs, sp, sex)
summarise(crab_groups,
          mean_fl_cw = mean(fl_cw_ratio), sd_fl_cw = sd(fl_cw_ratio),
          mean_rw_cl = mean(rw_cl_ratio), sd_rw_cl = sd(rw_cl_ratio))
```

The means of the ratio of the front lip differ by about 0.04 between the species,
which is about three to five times the standard deviation within a group. The means of the ratio
of the rear width differ by about 0.06 between the sexes, but the standard deviation of the
males is larger than that of the females, so the two sexes overlap more than the two species
do.

## What we take forward

The exploration has not answered our question, but it has told us how to answer it. The
absolute measurements are dominated by the size of the crabs and are of little use on their
own. Ratios of measurements describe the shape, and the two ratios above are good candidates
for the response variable: the width of the front lip relative to the carapace width for the
species, and the rear width relative to the carapace length for the sexes. Both are positive
continuous variables, so the Normal and LogNormal distributions of
[Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-continuous_measurements) and the Gamma
distribution of the [Supplement](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-gamma) (used in
Exercise 4 of the [Chapter 4 practical](../Chapter_4/Practicals/no_solution.qmd)) are all
possible models for them.

# The difference between the species {#sec-crabs-species}

We now apply the recipe for a fit of [Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-aic) to the
first half of our question: how well can we tell the two species apart? The response
variable is the ratio of the front lip to the carapace width, the ratio that separated the
species in @fig-crabs-ratios. In that figure, the males and the females of each species
have almost the same distribution of this ratio, so for this comparison we can ignore sex
and treat the 100 crabs of each species as one sample. This simplifies our life a lot:
we have two groups instead of four, and every model has fewer parameters. (If the sexes
differed in this ratio, we would have to include both factors in the model.)

We proceed in four steps. First, we choose a distribution for the ratio by comparing two
candidates with AIC, separately for each species. Second, we write a model in which the
difference between the means of the two species is itself a parameter, and use AIC to
decide whether we need to account for different variation within each species. Third, we
estimate the difference between species with its confidence intervals. Finally, we check
with a simulation that the estimate and its intervals behave as the theory of Chapter 4
promises.

## The model

Let $Y_i$ be the ratio of the front lip to the carapace width of crab $i$. Within each
species, we treat the ratios as i.i.d.: every crab was caught and measured once, and its
ratio tells us nothing about the ratio of the next crab. (Crabs caught on the same night or
on the same stretch of rock could be more alike than crabs caught far apart; we ignore this
here, and [Chapter 7](../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd) shows how such groups could be modelled.)

The ratio is a positive continuous variable, so we try two distributions that are made for
such variables: the Gamma distribution (see the
[Supplement](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-gamma)) and the LogNormal distribution of
[Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-continuous_measurements). As recommended in the
[Supplement](../Supplements/distributions.qmd), we parameterise both by their mean $\mu$.
For the second parameter we use the **coefficient of variation** (CV), the standard
deviation divided by the mean, $v=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}/\mu$. For positive measurements the
spread tends to grow with the mean (bigger things vary more in absolute terms), so the
relative variation is a natural way to describe it, and it lets us compare the two
species, whose means differ, on the same footing. Both distributions can be written with
$\mu$ and $v$:

- For the [Gamma distribution](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-gamma) the standard
  deviation is $v\mu$, and the shape is $k=1/v^2$, so the coefficient of variation is the
  $1/\sqrt{k}$ of the Supplement. The function `dgamma2()` of RTMBdist takes the mean and
  the standard deviation, so we give it `mean = mu` and `sd = cv * mu`.
- For the [LogNormal distribution](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-lognormal) the mean
  and the variance in the Supplement give $v^2=e^{\sigma^2}-1$, so

  $$
  \sigma^2=\log\left(1+v^2\right) \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mu_{\log}=\log(\mu)-\frac{\sigma^2}{2},
  $$

  where $\sigma$ (`sdlog`) and $\mu_{\log}$ (`meanlog`) are the standard deviation and the
  mean of $\log(Y)$, the arguments of `dlnorm()`.

## Gamma or LogNormal?

We load RTMB and RTMBdist as in Chapter 4 and split the ratios into the two species:

```{r}
#| message: false
# Load RTMB first and RTMBdist second.
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)

# Ratio of the front lip to the carapace width for each species (no units).
blue_ratio = crabs$fl_cw_ratio[crabs$sp == "B"]
orange_ratio = crabs$fl_cw_ratio[crabs$sp == "O"]
```

The two NLLs take the mean and the coefficient of variation on the log scale, because both
are positive ([Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-constraints)), and the ratios as
`x`. The LogNormal NLL converts $\mu$ and $v$ into `meanlog` and `sdlog` with the two
equations above:

```{r}
# Gamma model with mean mu and coefficient of variation cv.
gamma_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  mu = exp(log_mu)
  cv = exp(log_cv)
  -sum(dgamma2(x = x, mean = mu, sd = cv * mu, log = TRUE))
}

# LogNormal model with mean mu and coefficient of variation cv.
lognormal_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  mu = exp(log_mu)
  cv = exp(log_cv)
  # Parameters of the distribution of log(x).
  sdlog = sqrt(log(1 + cv^2))
  meanlog = log(mu) - sdlog^2 / 2
  -sum(dlnorm(x = x, meanlog = meanlog, sdlog = sdlog, log = TRUE))
}
```

We need four fits (two distributions for each of two species), and every fit repeats the
same two steps of the recipe: process the NLL with `MakeADFun()` and minimise it with
`optim()`. Instead of copying these lines four times, we put them in a function, as you
learnt to do in the Chapter 1 practical. The function `fit_ratio()` takes an NLL and the
ratios of one species, and returns the result of `optim()`. The starting values are a mean
of 0.4, read from @fig-crabs-ratios, and a coefficient of variation of 0.05, a rough
guess (any values from which the optimiser reaches the maximum will do):

```{r}
# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

# Process an NLL for the ratios x of one species and minimise it.
fit_ratio = function(nll, x) {
  obj = MakeADFun(
    cmb(nll, list(x = x)),
    list(log_mu = log(0.4), log_cv = log(0.05)),
    silent = TRUE
  )
  optim(par = obj$par, fn = obj$fn, gr = obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
}

blue_gamma_fit = fit_ratio(gamma_nll, blue_ratio)
blue_lognormal_fit = fit_ratio(lognormal_nll, blue_ratio)
orange_gamma_fit = fit_ratio(gamma_nll, orange_ratio)
orange_lognormal_fit = fit_ratio(lognormal_nll, orange_ratio)

# Convergence codes (0 = normal stop) and the Gamma estimates of mu and cv.
c(blue_gamma_fit$convergence, blue_lognormal_fit$convergence,
  orange_gamma_fit$convergence, orange_lognormal_fit$convergence)
rbind(exp(blue_gamma_fit$par), exp(blue_lognormal_fit$par))
rbind(exp(orange_gamma_fit$par), exp(orange_lognormal_fit$par))
```

All four fits converged. Before comparing the models, it is worth noticing how small the
coefficients of variation are: about 0.024 for the blue species and 0.027 for the orange
species, so the standard deviation of the ratio is less than 3% of its mean. We will come
back to this in a moment.

We compare the two distributions with AIC within each species (an AIC can only be compared
between models fitted to the same observations, so the blue and the orange crabs form two
separate comparisons). As in Chapter 4, the maximum log-likelihood is minus the element
`value` of the fit:

```{r}
# Maximised log-likelihood, number of parameters K and AIC of the four fits.
distribution_table = data.frame(
  species = c("blue", "blue", "orange", "orange"),
  distribution = c("Gamma", "LogNormal", "Gamma", "LogNormal"),
  K = 2,
  loglik = -c(blue_gamma_fit$value, blue_lognormal_fit$value,
              orange_gamma_fit$value, orange_lognormal_fit$value)
)
distribution_table$aic = 2 * distribution_table$K - 2 * distribution_table$loglik
distribution_table
```

The Gamma model has the lower AIC for the blue crabs and the LogNormal model for the orange
crabs, but the differences are 0.09 and 0.32 units, which means that the data cannot tell
the two distributions apart. (AICc would not change this: both models have the same
number of parameters and are fitted to the same number of crabs, so they receive the same
correction.) The reason is the small coefficient of variation. The Gamma and the LogNormal
distributions differ mostly in how skewed they are, and with a relative variation of 2–3%
both are nearly symmetric bell curves that are almost impossible to distinguish. We can
see this by drawing the fitted densities of the two distributions for each species with
`curve()`. The LogNormal density needs the conversion from $\mu$ and $v$ every time, so we
put it in a short function, `dlnorm_cv()`:

```{r}
#| label: fig-crabs-distributions
#| fig-cap: "Fitted Gamma (solid) and LogNormal (dashed) densities of the ratio of the front lip to the carapace width for the blue and the orange species."
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 6
# LogNormal density with mean mu and coefficient of variation cv.
dlnorm_cv = function(x, mu, cv) {
  sdlog = sqrt(log(1 + cv^2))
  dlnorm(x, meanlog = log(mu) - sdlog^2 / 2, sdlog = sdlog)
}

# Estimates of mu (first element) and cv (second element) of the four fits.
blue_gamma = exp(blue_gamma_fit$par)
blue_lognormal = exp(blue_lognormal_fit$par)
orange_gamma = exp(orange_gamma_fit$par)
orange_lognormal = exp(orange_lognormal_fit$par)

curve(dgamma2(x, mean = blue_gamma[1], sd = blue_gamma[2] * blue_gamma[1]),
      from = 0.37, to = 0.50, col = form_colours[1], lwd = 2,
      xlab = "Front lip / carapace width", ylab = "Density")
curve(dlnorm_cv(x, mu = blue_lognormal[1], cv = blue_lognormal[2]),
      add = TRUE, col = form_colours[1], lwd = 2, lty = 2)
curve(dgamma2(x, mean = orange_gamma[1], sd = orange_gamma[2] * orange_gamma[1]),
      add = TRUE, col = form_colours[2], lwd = 2)
curve(dlnorm_cv(x, mu = orange_lognormal[1], cv = orange_lognormal[2]),
      add = TRUE, col = form_colours[2], lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", legend = c("Gamma", "LogNormal"), lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")
```

For each species, the two estimated density functions lie on top of each other. So the
choice between them does not matter for our question, and we continue with
the Gamma distribution, because `dgamma2()` takes the mean and the standard deviation
directly and its NLL is a little simpler. (If you repeat the next steps with the LogNormal
distribution, you will get practically the same estimates and standard errors.) Note that
this is a conclusion about these data. For a variable with a larger relative variation,
the two distributions differ more in shape (both are skewed to the right, but not in the
same way), and the data may be able to tell them apart. Also note that, with such a small
variation, you could get away with a Normal distribution, because the probability of a
negative value would be extremely low. We stay with the Gamma distribution, though, because
we will not always be so lucky with our data.

## The difference between the means as a parameter

So far each species had its own mean. For our question, however, the interesting quantity
is the difference between the two means, and it is convenient to make that difference a
parameter of the model. We take the blue species as the reference (the "control") and
describe the orange species by how much its mean differs from it (the "effect"):

$$
\mu_i=\mu_{\mathrm{B}}+\delta\,o_i,
$$

where $\mu_i$ is the mean ratio of crab $i$, $\mu_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the mean ratio of the
blue species, $\delta$ is the difference between the mean ratio of the orange species and
that of the blue species, and $o_i$ is 1 if crab $i$ is orange and 0 if it is blue^[If you
have used `lm()`, this is how it codes a factor with two levels: the first level is the
reference, and the coefficient of the second level is its difference from the reference. In
machine learning and AI, distinguishing groups with such 0/1 variables is called "one-hot
encoding": the "hot" variable is the one that is switched on with a 1, while the others
stay "cold" at 0. Statisticians are not so good at marketing...]. For a blue crab the mean
is $\mu_{\mathrm{B}}$ and for an orange crab it is $\mu_{\mathrm{B}}+\delta$. This is only a
different way of writing the two means, so it does not change how well the model fits the
data. The advantage is that $\delta$ is now a
parameter: its estimate comes with a standard error from `sdreport()` and a likelihood
profile from `tmbprofile()`, which is exactly what we need to say how large the difference
is and how precisely we know it.

This also means that we do not need to fit a model without a difference ($\delta=0$, one
Gamma distribution for all the crabs) and compare it with AIC. That comparison would only
tell us whether a model with a difference is better than one without, which is the
question "is there a difference?" that we decided not to ask. The confidence interval of
$\delta$ tells us much more: which sizes of the difference the data support, and, as a
by-product, whether a difference of zero is among them. Whenever the question is about the
size of an effect, put the effect in the model as a parameter and look at its estimate and
interval, rather than at a comparison between a model with the effect and one without.

The mean $\mu_{\mathrm{B}}$ is positive, so we estimate its logarithm as before. The
difference $\delta$ is not transformed: we do not want to assume in advance which species
has the larger ratio, so $\delta$ must be allowed to take any value^[Strictly, the mean of
the orange crabs must stay positive, which would fail for $\delta<-\mu_{\mathrm{B}}$; with
ratios around 0.4 and a difference of a few hundredths, the optimiser never gets near that
value.]. In R, $o_i$ is a vector of zeros and ones, which we create by comparing the species
with `"O"` and turning the result into numbers:

```{r}
# 1 for an orange crab and 0 for a blue crab.
is_orange = as.numeric(crabs$sp == "O")
```

What about the variation within each species? We found a slightly larger coefficient of
variation for the orange crabs (0.027 against 0.024), and we have to decide whether both
species share one coefficient of variation or each has its own. This matters for our
question: the standard error of $\hat\delta$ depends on how variable the crabs of each
species are, so a model with the wrong variation could give us a misleading idea of how
precisely we know $\delta$. We write both models. The first one has a single parameter
`log_cv`; we also mark the data with `OBS()`, so that we can simulate from this model at
the end of the section, as in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-likelihood-uncertainty):

```{r}
# Gamma model with a difference delta between the mean ratios of the orange and the blue
# species, and one coefficient of variation for both species.
species_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  # Mark the data as observations, so that they can be simulated.
  x = OBS(x)
  mu = exp(log_mu_blue) + delta * is_orange
  cv = exp(log_cv)
  -sum(dgamma2(x = x, mean = mu, sd = cv * mu, log = TRUE))
}
```

The second model has one coefficient of variation per species. In the line for `cv`,
`c(log_cv_blue, log_cv_orange)` is a vector with the two parameters, and we select an
element of it for every crab by its position, as in the Chapter 1 practical. The position
is `is_orange + 1`, which is 1 for a blue crab and 2 for an orange crab, so every crab
gets the coefficient of variation of its own species and `cv` becomes a vector of 200
values:

```{r}
# The same model with one coefficient of variation per species.
species_cv_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  mu = exp(log_mu_blue) + delta * is_orange
  # Element 1 (blue) or 2 (orange) for every crab.
  cv = exp(c(log_cv_blue, log_cv_orange)[is_orange + 1])
  -sum(dgamma2(x = x, mean = mu, sd = cv * mu, log = TRUE))
}
```

Both models use the ratios of all 200 crabs and the vector `is_orange`. We fit them from
the same starting values as before, with $\delta=0$ (no difference) as the starting value
of the difference:

```{r}
# Data and starting values shared by both models.
species_data = list(x = crabs$fl_cw_ratio, is_orange = is_orange)
species_start = list(log_mu_blue = log(0.4), delta = 0, log_cv = log(0.05))

# One coefficient of variation.
species_obj = MakeADFun(cmb(species_nll, species_data), species_start, silent = TRUE)
species_fit = optim(par = species_obj$par, fn = species_obj$fn, gr = species_obj$gr,
                    method = "BFGS")

# One coefficient of variation per species.
species_cv_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(species_cv_nll, species_data),
  list(log_mu_blue = log(0.4), delta = 0, log_cv_blue = log(0.05),
       log_cv_orange = log(0.05)),
  silent = TRUE
)
species_cv_fit = optim(par = species_cv_obj$par, fn = species_cv_obj$fn,
                       gr = species_cv_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")

c(species_fit$convergence, species_cv_fit$convergence)
```

We compare the two models with AIC:

```{r}
# Maximised log-likelihood, number of parameters K and AIC of the two models.
species_table = data.frame(
  model = c("one CV", "one CV per species"),
  K = c(3, 4),
  loglik = -c(species_fit$value, species_cv_fit$value)
)
species_table$aic = 2 * species_table$K - 2 * species_table$loglik
species_table$delta_aic = species_table$aic - min(species_table$aic)
species_table
```

A separate coefficient of variation for each species raises the log-likelihood by less
than half a unit, which does not pay for the extra parameter, so the model with a single
coefficient of variation has the lower AIC (by 1.1 units; with AICc the difference would
be 1.2 units). In other words, the blue and the orange crabs seem to have very similar
coefficients of variation, and a second coefficient of variation is not worth its extra
parameter.

We can also set AIC aside and check directly whether the choice affects our answer, by
looking at the estimate of $\delta$ and its standard error in both models^[In recent
statistical discussions this is called a *multiverse analysis*: one evaluates the
consequences of the many small decisions that are specific to the data and tangential to
the question, but that could still influence the answer. In other fields it is called a
sensitivity analysis.]:

```{r}
# Estimate and standard error of delta in the two models with a difference.
rbind(one_cv = summary(sdreport(species_obj))["delta", ],
      cv_per_species = summary(sdreport(species_cv_obj))["delta", ])
```

The two models give the same estimate and almost the same standard error, so the choice
does not matter for our question and we continue with the simpler model, with one
coefficient of variation.

## How large is the difference?

The estimates and their standard errors come from `sdreport()`, as in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-wald-automation):

```{r}
# Estimates and standard errors on the scale that was optimised.
species_summary = summary(sdreport(species_obj))
species_summary
```

The parameter $\delta$ was not transformed, so its Wald interval is calculated directly as
the estimate plus and minus 1.96 standard errors. For the likelihood profile interval, we
profile `delta` with `TMB::tmbprofile()` and find the crossings of the cutoff with
`confint()`, as in
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-profile_intervals):

```{r}
# Wald interval for delta.
critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)
wald_delta = species_summary["delta", "Estimate"] +
  c(-1, 1) * critical_value * species_summary["delta", "Std. Error"]

# Likelihood profile interval for delta (confint() returns a matrix with one row).
species_profile_delta = TMB::tmbprofile(species_obj, name = "delta", trace = FALSE)
profile_delta = confint(species_profile_delta)[1, ]

rbind(wald_delta, profile_delta)
```

The estimated difference is $\hat\delta=0.0437$ and both intervals go from 0.041 to 0.047.
The two intervals agree to four decimals because, with 200 crabs, the log-likelihood of
$\delta$ is very close to a parabola, which is the condition under which the Wald interval
is accurate (Chapter 4). So the front lip of an orange crab is wider, relative to its
carapace, by about 0.044 times the carapace width. For a crab with a carapace 40 mm wide,
this is about 1.7 mm, which is easy to measure with callipers that read to 0.1 mm. The
interval is narrow compared with the difference itself, so the data determine the
difference precisely. It is also far from zero: the differences that the data support (at
the 95% level) lie between 0.041 and 0.047, so we know that the species differ without
fitting a model in which they do not.

Keep in mind what $\delta$ describes: the difference between the **means** of the two
species, that is, between the average blue crab and the average orange crab. The interval
tells us how precisely we know this difference between means, not how different two
individual crabs are. Individual crabs vary around the mean of their species, so a
particular orange crab can still have a smaller ratio than a particular blue crab (the two
distributions in @fig-crabs-distributions overlap a little).

## Checking the estimator by simulation

The standard error and both intervals rely on the large-sample results of
[Chapter 4](../Chapter_4/Theory.qmd#sec-mle_properties): approximately, the estimator is
unbiased, its standard deviation across hypothetical samples is the standard error that
`sdreport()` calculates, and a 95% interval contains the parameter in 95% of the samples.
With 100 crabs in each species we expect these approximations to be good, but we can check
them, because we can simulate data from our model with a value of $\delta$ that we know.

We simulate 1,000 hypothetical samples with the same design (100 blue and 100 orange
crabs) from the fitted model, using the estimates as the parameters. We marked the data in
`species_nll()` with `OBS()`, so `species_obj$simulate()` draws one hypothetical sample of
200 ratios. Each sample is then fitted by maximum likelihood, starting from the same values
as the fit to the real data, and we keep the estimate of $\delta$ and its standard error:

```{r}
# Hypothetical samples of 100 blue and 100 orange crabs from the fitted model.
set.seed(seed = 417)
n_samples = 1000
sim_delta = rep(NA, n_samples)
sim_se = rep(NA, n_samples)
for (i in seq_len(n_samples)) {
  # One hypothetical sample at the estimates for the crabs.
  sim_ratio = species_obj$simulate(species_fit$par)$x

  # Maximum likelihood, starting from the same values as for the crabs.
  sim_obj = MakeADFun(
    cmb(species_nll, list(x = sim_ratio, is_orange = is_orange)),
    species_start,
    silent = TRUE
  )
  sim_fit = optim(par = sim_obj$par, fn = sim_obj$fn, gr = sim_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
  sim_summary = summary(sdreport(sim_obj))
  sim_delta[i] = sim_summary["delta", "Estimate"]
  sim_se[i] = sim_summary["delta", "Std. Error"]
}
```

The value of $\delta$ used to simulate is the estimate for the crabs. We compare it with
the mean of the 1,000 estimates (bias), compare the standard deviation of the estimates
with the average standard error, and calculate the fraction of Wald intervals that contain
it (coverage):

```{r}
# Value of delta used to simulate.
delta_sim = species_fit$par[["delta"]]

# Bias: mean of the estimates minus the value used to simulate.
mean(sim_delta) - delta_sim

# Standard deviation of the estimates and average standard error.
c(sd_estimates = sd(sim_delta), mean_se = mean(sim_se))

# Coverage of the 95% Wald interval.
sim_lower = sim_delta - critical_value * sim_se
sim_upper = sim_delta + critical_value * sim_se
mean(sim_lower < delta_sim & delta_sim < sim_upper)
```

The estimator behaves as promised. The bias is $-0.00003$, less than 0.1% of $\delta$ and
negligible compared with the standard error. The standard deviation of the estimates
(0.00151) is close to the average standard error (0.00155), so `sdreport()` describes the
uncertainty of $\hat\delta$ well. The Wald interval contains the value used to simulate in
95.4% of the samples, as close to 95% as we can expect from 1,000 samples (with another
seed the coverage would be a little different). We did not check the profile interval,
because for these data it is practically the same as the Wald interval.

Keep in mind what this simulation does and does not tell us. The hypothetical samples were
drawn from our model, so the simulation shows that maximum likelihood estimation and the
intervals work well when the model is the data generating process, for this design and
sample size. It cannot tell us whether the model describes the real crabs well. AIC only
ranks the candidate models, and [Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Theory.qmd) introduces checks of
how well a fitted model describes the data, though the final decision on "how good is good
enough" remains with the scientist.

# The difference between the sexes {#sec-crabs-sexes}

For the second half of our question, how well we can tell the two sexes apart, we follow
the same recipe with the ratio of the rear width to the carapace length, the ratio that
separated the sexes in @fig-crabs-ratios. Two things are different from the comparison of
the species. First, in the exploration the standard deviation of this ratio was clearly
larger for the males than for the females, so the question of whether each group needs its
own coefficient of variation will matter more. Second, this time we keep both factors in
the model. For the species we ignored sex, because the two sexes had practically the same
distribution of the front lip ratio. The same figure suggests that the two species hardly
differ in the rear width ratio, so we could ignore the species here as well. Instead, we
show a more complex alternative: we include the difference between the species as a second
parameter and let its estimate tell us how much it matters.

## Gamma or LogNormal, again

We repeat the comparison of the two distributions, now separately for each sex. Within a
sex we pool the two species, because in @fig-crabs-ratios they have almost the same
distribution of this ratio (the model below will check this). The two NLLs and
`fit_ratio()` work for any ratio, so we only need the ratios of each sex:

```{r}
# Ratio of the rear width to the carapace length for each sex (no units).
female_ratio = crabs$rw_cl_ratio[crabs$sex == "F"]
male_ratio = crabs$rw_cl_ratio[crabs$sex == "M"]

female_gamma_fit = fit_ratio(gamma_nll, female_ratio)
female_lognormal_fit = fit_ratio(lognormal_nll, female_ratio)
male_gamma_fit = fit_ratio(gamma_nll, male_ratio)
male_lognormal_fit = fit_ratio(lognormal_nll, male_ratio)

# Convergence codes and the Gamma estimates of mu and cv for each sex.
c(female_gamma_fit$convergence, female_lognormal_fit$convergence,
  male_gamma_fit$convergence, male_lognormal_fit$convergence)
rbind(female = exp(female_gamma_fit$par), male = exp(male_gamma_fit$par))
```

All four fits converged. The mean ratio of the males is lower than that of the females, and
their coefficient of variation (about 0.064) is almost twice that of the females (about
0.034). We compare the two distributions with AIC within each sex:

```{r}
# Maximised log-likelihood, number of parameters K and AIC of the four fits.
sex_distribution_table = data.frame(
  sex = c("female", "female", "male", "male"),
  distribution = c("Gamma", "LogNormal", "Gamma", "LogNormal"),
  K = 2,
  loglik = -c(female_gamma_fit$value, female_lognormal_fit$value,
              male_gamma_fit$value, male_lognormal_fit$value)
)
sex_distribution_table$aic = 2 * sex_distribution_table$K -
  2 * sex_distribution_table$loglik
sex_distribution_table
```

This time the LogNormal distribution has the lower AIC in both sexes, but by only 0.06
units for the females and 0.72 units for the males. The relative variation is larger than
for the front lip ratio, but still small enough for both distributions to be nearly
symmetric, so the data cannot tell them apart and we continue with the Gamma distribution.

## Two differences in one model

We describe the four groups with the blue females as the reference and two differences:

$$
\mu_i=\mu_{\mathrm{BF}}+\delta_{\mathrm{M}}\,m_i+\delta_{\mathrm{O}}\,o_i,
$$

where $\mu_{\mathrm{BF}}$ is the mean ratio of the blue females, $m_i$ is 1 if crab $i$ is
a male and 0 if it is a female, $o_i$ is 1 for an orange crab as before,
$\delta_{\mathrm{M}}$ is the difference between the mean ratio of the males and that of the
females, and $\delta_{\mathrm{O}}$ is the difference between the mean ratio of the orange
and that of the blue species. The mean of the blue females is $\mu_{\mathrm{BF}}$, that of
the blue males $\mu_{\mathrm{BF}}+\delta_{\mathrm{M}}$, that of the orange females
$\mu_{\mathrm{BF}}+\delta_{\mathrm{O}}$, and that of the orange males
$\mu_{\mathrm{BF}}+\delta_{\mathrm{M}}+\delta_{\mathrm{O}}$. Note that this model is not the
same as four separate means, since we describe four groups with three parameters. The
differences simply add up, which is why such a model is called **additive**, and it assumes
that the difference between the sexes is the same in both species. Whether the sexual
dimorphism differs between the species could be checked with a third difference that
applies only to the orange males, $\delta_{\mathrm{MO}}\,m_i\,o_i$. I tried it and found an
estimate of 0.0009 with a standard error of 0.0055, that is, no sign that the dimorphism
differs between the species, so I leave it out to keep the model simple.

As for the species, we create the vector of zeros and ones for the sexes:

```{r}
# 1 for a male and 0 for a female.
is_male = as.numeric(crabs$sex == "M")
```

We write two models again, one with a single coefficient of variation and one with a
coefficient of variation per sex, which selects an element of
`c(log_cv_female, log_cv_male)` with `is_male + 1` in the same way as before:

```{r}
# Gamma model with differences between the sexes and between the species, and one
# coefficient of variation for all crabs.
sex_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  mu = exp(log_mu_blue_female) + delta_male * is_male + delta_orange * is_orange
  cv = exp(log_cv)
  -sum(dgamma2(x = x, mean = mu, sd = cv * mu, log = TRUE))
}

# The same model with one coefficient of variation per sex.
sex_cv_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  mu = exp(log_mu_blue_female) + delta_male * is_male + delta_orange * is_orange
  # Element 1 (female) or 2 (male) for every crab.
  cv = exp(c(log_cv_female, log_cv_male)[is_male + 1])
  -sum(dgamma2(x = x, mean = mu, sd = cv * mu, log = TRUE))
}
```

Both models use the ratios of all 200 crabs and the two vectors of zeros and ones. We start
again with no differences:

```{r}
# Data shared by both models.
sex_data = list(x = crabs$rw_cl_ratio, is_male = is_male, is_orange = is_orange)

# One coefficient of variation.
sex_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(sex_nll, sex_data),
  list(log_mu_blue_female = log(0.4), delta_male = 0, delta_orange = 0,
       log_cv = log(0.05)),
  silent = TRUE
)
sex_fit = optim(par = sex_obj$par, fn = sex_obj$fn, gr = sex_obj$gr, method = "BFGS")

# One coefficient of variation per sex.
sex_cv_obj = MakeADFun(
  cmb(sex_cv_nll, sex_data),
  list(log_mu_blue_female = log(0.4), delta_male = 0, delta_orange = 0,
       log_cv_female = log(0.05), log_cv_male = log(0.05)),
  silent = TRUE
)
sex_cv_fit = optim(par = sex_cv_obj$par, fn = sex_cv_obj$fn, gr = sex_cv_obj$gr,
                   method = "BFGS")

c(sex_fit$convergence, sex_cv_fit$convergence)
```

And we compare them with AIC:

```{r}
# Maximised log-likelihood, number of parameters K and AIC of the two models.
sex_table = data.frame(
  model = c("one CV", "one CV per sex"),
  K = c(4, 5),
  loglik = -c(sex_fit$value, sex_cv_fit$value)
)
sex_table$aic = 2 * sex_table$K - 2 * sex_table$loglik
sex_table$delta_aic = sex_table$aic - min(sex_table$aic)
sex_table
```

This time the answer is clear: a coefficient of variation per sex lowers the AIC by 34
units (AICc changes this by about 0.1 units). The males vary much more than the females,
relative to their mean, and a single coefficient of variation cannot describe both sexes.
Does this choice affect our estimates of the differences? We look at both differences in
both models:

```{r}
# Estimates and standard errors of the two differences in both models.
summary(sdreport(sex_obj))[c("delta_male", "delta_orange"), ]
summary(sdreport(sex_cv_obj))[c("delta_male", "delta_orange"), ]
```

The estimates are practically the same in both models (thanks to the balanced design, the
estimate of $\delta_{\mathrm{M}}$ does not depend on the choice at all). The standard error
of $\hat\delta_{\mathrm{M}}$ hardly changes, but that of $\hat\delta_{\mathrm{O}}$ is about
15% larger in the model with one coefficient of variation. So in this case, ignoring that
the coefficient of variation differs between males and females would have made us
underestimate how precisely we know the difference between the species. We continue with
the model with one coefficient of variation per sex.

## How large are the differences between the sexes?

As before, the estimates and their standard errors come from `sdreport()`:

```{r}
# Estimates and standard errors of the model with one CV per sex.
sex_summary = summary(sdreport(sex_cv_obj))
sex_summary
```

Neither difference was transformed, so we calculate their Wald intervals directly:

```{r}
# Wald intervals for the difference between the sexes and between the species.
wald_male = sex_summary["delta_male", "Estimate"] +
  c(-1, 1) * critical_value * sex_summary["delta_male", "Std. Error"]
wald_orange = sex_summary["delta_orange", "Estimate"] +
  c(-1, 1) * critical_value * sex_summary["delta_orange", "Std. Error"]
rbind(wald_male, wald_orange)
```

The likelihood profile intervals from `TMB::tmbprofile()` differ from these by less than
0.0001 (you can check this by adapting the code of the previous section), for the same
reason as before: with 200 crabs, the log-likelihood of each difference is very close to a
parabola. The estimated difference between the sexes is
$\hat\delta_{\mathrm{M}}=-0.062$, with an interval from $-0.067$ to $-0.056$: the rear of
a male is narrower, relative to the length of its carapace, by about 0.062 times the
carapace length. For a crab with a carapace 30 mm long (close to the average of the data),
this is about 1.9 mm.

The estimated difference between the species is $\hat\delta_{\mathrm{O}}=-0.003$, with an
interval from $-0.008$ to $0.002$. This interval tells us two things. It includes zero, so
the data are compatible with no difference between the species. More importantly, both of
its ends are small: whatever the difference between the species is, it is at most about an
eighth of the difference between the sexes. This second part is something that a p-value or
a comparison of models with and without the difference could not tell us, because they
focus on a yes/no answer. So,
for this ratio, the species can safely be ignored, as the exploration suggested, and because
the design is balanced, ignoring it would not change our estimate of $\delta_{\mathrm{M}}$.

We do not repeat the simulation of the previous section for this model. The design is the
same and the estimators are the same kind, so we expect them to behave as well as before,
but if you want to check it, you can adapt the loop of the previous section (remember to
mark the data with `OBS()` in `sex_cv_nll()`).

To see what the differences in the means and in the variation mean for individual crabs,
we draw the fitted densities of the four groups. The means of the groups follow from the
equation above and the standard deviations from the coefficients of variation of the two
sexes:

```{r}
#| label: fig-crabs-sexes
#| fig-cap: "Fitted Gamma densities of the ratio of the rear width to the carapace length for the females (solid) and the males (dashed) of the blue and the orange species, from the model with one coefficient of variation per sex."
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 6
# Means of the four groups and coefficients of variation of the two sexes.
sex_par = sex_cv_fit$par
mu_blue_female = exp(sex_par[["log_mu_blue_female"]])
mu_blue_male = mu_blue_female + sex_par[["delta_male"]]
mu_orange_female = mu_blue_female + sex_par[["delta_orange"]]
mu_orange_male = mu_blue_male + sex_par[["delta_orange"]]
cv_female = exp(sex_par[["log_cv_female"]])
cv_male = exp(sex_par[["log_cv_male"]])

curve(dgamma2(x, mean = mu_blue_female, sd = cv_female * mu_blue_female),
      from = 0.29, to = 0.49, col = form_colours[1], lwd = 2,
      xlab = "Rear width / carapace length", ylab = "Density")
curve(dgamma2(x, mean = mu_blue_male, sd = cv_male * mu_blue_male),
      add = TRUE, col = form_colours[1], lwd = 2, lty = 2)
curve(dgamma2(x, mean = mu_orange_female, sd = cv_female * mu_orange_female),
      add = TRUE, col = form_colours[2], lwd = 2)
curve(dgamma2(x, mean = mu_orange_male, sd = cv_male * mu_orange_male),
      add = TRUE, col = form_colours[2], lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("Female", "Male"), lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")
```

The curves of the two species lie almost on top of each other, as the small
$\hat\delta_{\mathrm{O}}$ suggests. The curves of the two sexes, on the other hand, have
very different shapes: the females are concentrated in a narrow range, while the males are
spread over a much wider one, and the upper tail of the males reaches into the range of the
females. So the overlap between the sexes is larger than the overlap between the species in
@fig-crabs-distributions, and it is one-sided: it comes from males with a ratio as high as
that of a female.

The data suggest a reason for the larger variation of the males. If you calculate the
ratio for males of different sizes, you will find that it decreases as they grow, from
about 0.42 in males with a carapace shorter than 20 mm, close to the females, to about 0.34
in males with a carapace longer than 40 mm, whereas in females it changes little. In other
words, small males have the proportions of females. Our model ignores the size of the crab,
so this change appears as extra variation among the males. Describing how the ratio changes
with size is a question of allometry, and it needs the response curves of Chapters 5 to 7.

# The answer to our question {#sec-crabs-answer}

We asked to what extent we can tell apart the two species and the two sexes of these crabs
from a few measurements taken with callipers, and our answer has two parts.

The species differ in the ratio of the front lip to the carapace width. The mean ratio of
the orange crabs is larger than that of the blue crabs by 0.044 (95% confidence interval
from 0.041 to 0.047), the same in both sexes, which for a crab with a carapace 40 mm wide
is about 1.7 mm. Within each species the ratio varies little (its standard deviation is
2–3% of its mean), so the distributions of the two species overlap only a little (@fig-crabs-distributions).
This is a very different picture from that of any single measurement
(@fig-crabs-boxplots), which on its own would be almost useless because of the large
variation in actual sizes within each group.

The sexes differ in the ratio of the rear width to the carapace length. The mean ratio of
the males is smaller than that of the females by 0.062 (from 0.056 to 0.067), the same in
both species, which for a crab with a carapace 30 mm long is about 1.9 mm. This difference
is larger than the difference between the species, but the males vary about twice as much
as the females, so the two sexes overlap more (@fig-crabs-sexes).

Both parts of the answer rest on the model: we treated the crabs as independent, described
each group by a Gamma distribution with a mean and a coefficient of variation, and judged
the overlap of the groups by eye from the fitted distributions.

# Comparison with Campbell and Mahon (1974) {#sec-crabs-paper}

Campbell and Mahon answered the question with **canonical analysis**, a multivariate
method that finds the combinations of all five measurements that best separate the groups,
in the sense that the differences between the means of the groups are as large as possible
compared with the variation within them. It is beyond this course, but its results can be
compared with ours.

Their first combination, which separated the species, was a contrast between the carapace
width on one side and the width of the front lip and the depth of the body on the other:
the blue crabs have a wider carapace relative to their front lip than the orange crabs.
Their second combination, which separated the sexes, was a contrast between the carapace
length and the rear width: males have a longer carapace relative to their rear width than
females. These are the same differences in shape that our two ratios describe, in the same
directions. The two ratios we chose by looking at the scatter plots of @fig-crabs-pairs
capture most of what their method found by combining all the measurements (their
combination for the species also used the depth of the body, which we did not).

Their conclusions about overlap also agree with ours. Each of the five measurements on its
own overlapped almost completely between the groups, as in @fig-crabs-boxplots. Their
plots of the front lip against the carapace width and of the carapace length against the
rear width (the two pairs of measurements behind our ratios) showed very little overlap
between the species and minimal overlap between the sexes, with a few crabs that would be
identified incorrectly. When they allowed the variation to differ between the groups, they
also found that the blue males were less well separated from the females than the orange
males, in line with our finding that the overlap between the sexes comes from the males.

Where their method went further is in combining all five measurements into a rule that
assigns individual crabs to a species and a sex. In this case study I focused on comparing
the groups through their means and variation, which is the most common kind of question in
ecological research. If I instead wanted a rule to assign individual crabs to their group,
I would look at classification techniques from machine learning, which have made great
progress since the 1970s, when this study was done.
